title: Algebra and Numbers
objective: After this level you can explain how al-Khwarizmi and others shaped mathematics.
summary: Al-Khwarizmi's al-jabr book named algebra and his Latin name gave us algorithm. The numerals came from India, through the Islamic world, to Europe.

cards.headline: Say “algorithm” and you’re saying a Baghdad scholar’s name.
cards.body: Say “algebra” and you’re quoting the title of his book. Meet al-Khwarizmi, and the numbers he helped carry west.

cards.headline: A book about balancing
cards.body: Al-Khwarizmi, who lived from about 780 to 850, worked at the House of Wisdom you met in Level 61. Around 825 he wrote a book on calculating by al-jabr and balancing. Al-jabr, “restoring”, meant moving a subtracted term to the other side of an equation; balancing cancelled what matched on both sides. Its Latin translation in the 12th century gave us the word algebra. If you’ve ever moved x to the other side, you’ve done al-jabr.

cards.headline: Numbers from India
cards.body: The digits you use every day originated in India in the 6th or 7th century. Al-Khwarizmi wrote a book of arithmetic with them, which survives in Latin as Algoritmi de numero Indorum, “Al-Khwarizmi Concerning the Hindu Art of Reckoning”. That Latin spelling of his name, Algoritmi, became our word algorithm. Hence “Hindu-Arabic” numerals: invented in India, carried by the Islamic world.

mascot.line: People say “Arabic numerals”. Keep the whole trip: invented in India, carried by the Islamic world.

cards.headline: Into Europe
cards.body: Mathematicians of the Islamic world, especially al-Khwarizmi and al-Kindi, brought the numerals to Europe about the 12th century. Even so, when Fibonacci published his Liber abaci in 1202, few Europeans knew them. He had learned calculation from an Arab master in North Africa, and his book spread the system. Next time you do long division, thank a chain of scholars from India to Pisa.
cards.callout: India invented them; the Islamic world carried them; Europe adopted them

cards.headline: Algebra and numbers: known
learned: Al-Khwarizmi worked at the House of Wisdom
His al-jabr book gave us the word algebra
His Latin name gave us algorithm
Our digits came from India through the Islamic world

questions.prompt: The word “algebra” comes from al-Khwarizmi’s book. What did its key term, al-jabr, mean?

options.label: Counting
options.rationale: It named a step in solving equations.

options.label: Dividing
options.rationale: It meant moving a term across.

options.label: Measuring
options.rationale: It was about equations, not lengths.

questions.explanation: Al-jabr meant “restoring”: moving a subtracted term to the other side of an equation.

questions.prompt: Why are the digits we use called Hindu-Arabic numerals?

options.label: Arab traders invented them in Baghdad
Invented in India, carried west by the Islamic world
Invented in Rome, then improved in India
options.rationale: Roman numerals are a different system.

options.label: They mix Hindi words with Arabic letters
options.rationale: The name tells their route, not their script.

questions.explanation: The numerals originated in India, and scholars of the Islamic world such as al-Khwarizmi carried them west.

questions.prompt: Al-Khwarizmi’s numerals reached Europe through the Islamic world. From Level 49, which route for Arabic science do historians doubt?

options.label: Through Sicily
options.rationale: Level 49 names Sicily as a likely route.

options.label: Through Spain
options.rationale: Spain, like Sicily, was a likely route.

questions.explanation: Unlike Sicily and Spain, the crusader states do not seem to have carried Arabic science west; the numerals came through mathematicians of the Islamic world.
